tier_reason: Upgraded from B: the arXiv paper is a Google preprint (not peer reviewed) but states CPU (Xeon E5-2690 v3), compiler (Clang r331746) and flags (-O3 -std=gnu++11), and the benchmark code is public in the repo (randen_benchmark.cc, built by Makefile with clang++ -O3 -mavx2 -maes) and runs against std <random> mt19937_64 and pcg64.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper: Clang r331746 -O3 -std=gnu++11; repo Makefile: clang++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-pic -mavx2 -maes (README: GCC 7.3 up to 1.6x and Clang 4.0.1 up to 1.3x more cycles/byte)
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 (x86); also POWER8e
corrections.claimed_speedup: README x86: microbenchmark 1.54 cpb vs mt19937_64 1.79 and pcg64_c32 0.78 (PCG faster); reservoir sampling 2.60 cpb vs mt19937_64 2.82 and pcg64_c32 3.03. Paper: geometric mean over applied tasks about 1.1x faster than Mersenne Twister on x86 and PPC; PCG fastest on x86 (paper's shuffle and reservoir tables show PCG ~1.2x faster than Randen)
corrections.caveats: Modest win over std::mt19937_64 (~1.1x geomean, ~1.16x in microbenchmark derived from page data); slower than PCG in microbenchmark and most paper tasks; README reservoir table disagrees with paper's (README has Randen ahead of PCG); standard library used for mt19937_64 not stated; repo archived 2023-06-12, last commit 2018-10-05; algorithm lives on in Abseil's absl::random

notes: Paper is self-published (Google), so B was not justified on peer review, but full methodology plus public bench code earns A. Stdlib implementation not stated, baseline_stdlib left empty.

tier_reason: Tier changes from B (paper is only submitted to ACM TOMS, not peer reviewed) to A: the C++ comparison code is public (benchmark/TimeDistCpp.cpp, std::mt19937_64 + std uniform/normal distributions), the CPU is stated (i5-1335U), the compiler is clang, and the flags come from the repo build (meson release via scripts/meson-setup.sh, -ffp-model=precise -ffp-contract=off).

corrections.baseline: C++ std <random> (std::mt19937_64 + std::uniform_real_distribution / std::normal_distribution), NumPy, Base-R, Julia, oneMKL
corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Table 8 (Linux workstation, clang), ns/value: U(0,1) Randompack 0.42 vs C++ std 6.3 (~15x, derived from page data), NumPy 1.8, Julia 0.7, MKL 0.5; N(0,1) Randompack 1.4 vs C++ std 14.3 (~10x, derived from page data), NumPy 8.9, Julia 1.4, MKL 2.3
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang (version not stated in paper; gcc 1-16% slower, icx 6% slower); meson buildtype=release (via scripts/meson-setup.sh) with -ffp-model=precise -ffp-contract=off; C++ bench built with -U_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
corrections.caveats: Paper submitted to ACM TOMS (April 2026), not yet peer reviewed; first-party measurement; standard library implementation and clang version for the C++ column not stated; std::normal_distribution and mt19937_64 are known-slow baselines, while Julia and MKL are close; meson.build default buildtype is debug (the setup script and docs use release); 3 stars

notes: Corrected the claim wording: the record's '15x slower' meant C++ std is ~15x slower. Commits page blocked by robots.txt, so last_commit comes from the CHANGELOG date.

tier_reason: arXiv preprint by the author (not peer reviewed). It compares against xoshiro and PCG mainly through cycle counts and output latency from assembly analysis (g++ 4.8.4 -S -O3). Its only wall-clock table (Xeon E5-2643 v3) times RomuMono32 combinations and no baselines.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper tables: RomuTrio/RomuQuad/RomuDuo 3 cycles, 0 output latency vs xoshiro256++ 3 cycles, 3-cycle latency and pcg-xsh-rs 9 cycles, 7 latency; RomuQuad32 and RomuTrio32 3 cycles, 0 latency vs xoshiro128** 5 cycles, 5 latency; RomuMono32 4 cycles, 1 latency vs pcg-xsh-rr 4 cycles, 4 latency. The text says RomuMono32 matches pcg-xsh-rr quality with 3 arithmetic ops vs 7
corrections.caveats: Cycle and latency figures come from assembly analysis, not measured throughput against baselines; the paper's only timing table (5e9 calls, Xeon E5-2643 v3) covers just RomuMono32 combos; author-run preprint; source code is printed in the paper and served at romu-random.org/code.c (site TLS certificate expired, not opened); no license statement found; no official repo (Rust, .NET and R ports exist)

notes: The paper prints the generator code inline, so has_code was set to true. Usability stays reference because no license was found. A future search could look for an official licensed source.
